Evaluate, improve, repeat: the loop inside RL algorithms

The loop of evaluation and improvement inside most reinforcement learning methods, worked through on the cliff grid and traced from dynamic programming to AlphaGo Zero.

October 23, 20264 min readUpdated October 27, 2026

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Take a 4 × 12 grid. You start at S in the bottom-left corner, the goal G sits in the bottom-right, and the ten cells between them along the bottom edge are a cliff. Every move costs −1. Stepping off the cliff costs −100 and puts you back at S. We discount with γ = 0.99: the next reward counts fully, and each move after that multiplies its weight by 0.99. Now drop in a robot that picks each of its four moves with probability ¼. How good is it? Score a move by adding what it pays now to 0.99 times the value of wherever it lands, then average over the four moves. Each cell's value depends on its neighbors' values this way, so we get 37 equations, one for each cell the robot can stand in, and we solve them together. (We can do that because we know the model: where every move lands and what it pays.) The robot does terribly. Its value at S, the expected discounted return from S, written vπ(S), is about −1072.

So how do we get from this walker to the best route? Trying every policy is out of the question: four moves in each of 37 cells gives 437 ≈ 1.9 × 1022 deterministic policies. Here is what works instead. At each cell, try all four moves on paper: take that move once, then follow the old random policy afterward. Pick whichever scores best. Do this in every cell, and we have our new policy. Then evaluate that policy and go again. Sutton and Barto call this loop of evaluation and improvement generalized policy iteration (GPI), and they point out that most RL algorithms are this same loop with different parts plugged in. At S, going up scores about −1002 and the other three moves score worse, so the new policy goes up. Sounds promising. Where does it actually end up? The board follows it, top to bottom.

I think the wall trap in panel 3 is the nicest part of this example: we made the robot better in every cell, and starting from S it still never reaches the goal. Improvement only promises a higher value, and a wall that costs −1 forever pays better than the cliff. Five more rounds turn the trap into the 13-move walk along the cliff edge, which you can compare with the route Q-learning learned in the Q-learning post.

Everything above used the model. Now suppose we don't know where each move leads. We have to try it. Monte Carlo waits until a run ends and averages the discounted totals of repeated runs. Sarsa and Q-learning update after each move instead: they use the reward just observed plus a discounted estimate of what comes next. The loop stays the same, and the assessment becomes an estimate from experience. AlphaGo Zero makes the loop especially easy to see. Its network suggests moves, then tree search looks ahead to find better ones. Training teaches the network to imitate those search results and predict who wins the self-play games, so search improves the play and training puts that improvement back into the network. Sutton and Barto file it under policy iteration. The actor–critic row is my own reading: the textbook presents actor–critic apart from GPI, while Haarnoja et al. (2018) connect typical actor–critic derivations to policy iteration. So when you meet a new RL algorithm, ask three things: how does it assess the policy, how does it improve it, and how much assessing happens before each improvement?

Full round record, tie rule and sources

The numbers come from python3 scripts/rl_gpi_figures.py in the blog repository, which solves each policy's 37 equations directly. Values are rounded to two decimals.

The first greedy policy breaks ties in the order up, right, down, left, and all 24 priority orders give the same table. Later ties keep the current move, which stops the policy from cycling between equally good moves (Sutton and Barto, Exercise 4.4). Sutton and Barto also show that policy evaluation can be cut short in several ways and policy iteration still converges. In general, value iteration converges in the limit, and the exact result after 14 sweeps is specific to this grid.

Sources: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, second edition, MIT Press, 2018. Chapters 3 and 4 cover the Bellman equations, policy and value iteration and GPI, and the GPI diagram in panel 5 is adapted from them. Chapter 5 covers Monte Carlo control. Chapter 6 covers Sarsa and Q-learning, and it ties Q-learning to GPI in its introduction and conclusion. Chapters 13 and 14 cover actor–critic, Chapter 16 covers AlphaGo Zero, and Chapter 17 discusses GPI and actor–critic separately. Silver et al., Nature, 2017 (paper, author version). Haarnoja et al., ICML 2018 (arXiv). Part of the RL series.
